name: Blow dryer + round brush

lead: A blow dryer pushes heated air through hair while a round brush adds tension and curve, lifting the roots and setting volume. People use the pair for a fuller, shaped result that air-drying does not give.

Heat evaporates water and temporarily breaks hydrogen bonds in hair keratin, and hair cooled in a lifted or curved shape re-forms them in that shape, holding the style until moisture returns. Grooming communities recommend it for fine and thinning hair, where lift at the crown and hairline can make hair look denser.

paras: Users towel-dry, apply a heat protectant, then dry hair in sections while pulling it up and around the brush, finishing with a cool pass to set the shape. Technique matters more than equipment price. The result lasts until the next wash or humidity.

Heat damage is the main documented concern; studies on hair tresses report lifted and cracked cuticles at high temperatures. Keeping the dryer moving and at a distance, towel-drying first and using heat protectants are reported to reduce harm.

angle.text: Users blow-dry with a round brush to add root lift and body that air-drying does not give, a common route to a thicker-looking style. Heat and tension reset temporary hydrogen bonds so hair holds a lifted shape until the next wash. Frequent high heat can damage the cuticle.

lead: A blow dryer (hair dryer) blows warm or hot air over hair, and a round brush is a cylindrical brush that holds hair under tension and curve as it dries. Used together they add lift at the roots and body that air-drying does not usually give, which is why the pairing is a staple of styling for fine or thinning hair and for polished, fuller-looking hair in general. Wikipedia explains that dryers speed up the formation of temporary hydrogen bonds in each strand, which hold a hairstyle until moisture or washing breaks them [1].

The technique is the basis of the salon blowout, in which hair is dried smooth and voluminous with a dryer and brush. Wikipedia's hair-straightening article describes a dryer with a comb attachment or round brush as a way to straighten hair without chemicals, and notes that the effect lasts only until moisture returns the hair to its natural texture [2]. A chain of salons built entirely around the service, Drybar, grew from a 2010 startup to more than 100 locations by late 2018 according to Wikipedia [3].

Heat is the main documented concern: a 2025 laboratory study on hair tresses found lifted cuticles, lower surface water-repellence and higher protein release after a simulated month of daily dryer use [4]. Wikipedia's hair-care and straightening articles likewise say repeated or prolonged heat can damage hair and recommend low to medium heat settings [2][5]. No clinical study of blow-drying with a round brush as a method of looking thicker or more attractive was identified.

paras: Most hair dryers contain a heating element and a fan, usually driven by a universal motor. Wikipedia reports that many modern models use ceramic heating elements for rapid heat, include a cool-shot button that blows unheated air to help set a style and reduce frizz, and offer ionic operation, which is claimed to reduce static although its effectiveness is debated [1]. Attachments include diffusers, concentrator nozzles and comb nozzles. Diffusers are described as suited to fine, coloured, permed or naturally curly hair, giving gentler drying and more volume, while concentrators narrow the airflow for faster drying [1].
A hot-air brush combines a dryer and a round brush in one tool, in rotating and static versions [1]. Hood and bonnet dryers, which are mainly salon equipment, are a separate category [1].

Wikipedia's hairbrush article describes round brushes as used with a blow dryer to add fullness and movement and as suited to medium-length hair; some have a metal or ceramic base that heats during drying and helps shape the hair [6]. Other designs include vent brushes, which let air flow between the bristles, cushion brushes, paddle brushes (used for straightening and taming flyaways while blow-drying), detanglers and boar-bristle brushes, whose tightly spaced bristles increase tension to smooth the hair [6]. Bristle materials across brush types include boar, horsehair, nylon, stainless steel and goat hair [6]. The same article notes that straight hair usually looks smoother when brushed while curly hair tends to expand when brushed dry [6].
Round-brush dryers, which build the brush into the dryer, come in rotating versions, whose barrels turn automatically, and static versions [1].

According to Wikipedia, the French stylist Alexandre Godefroy invented the first hair dryer in 1888, a large seated salon dryer attached to a gas stove's chimney pipe, and Gabriel Kazanjian received a US patent for a dryer in 1911 [1]. Handheld household dryers reached the market around 1920, made by companies including National Stamping and Electric Works, Racine Universal Motor Company and Hamilton Beach. Early models weighed about 1 kg, drew about 100 W and posed overheating and electrocution risks [1]. The bonnet dryer reached consumers in 1951, rigid-hood dryers followed in the 1950s, GEC moved the motor inside the casing in 1954, and plastic casings and better motors made dryers lighter in the 1960s [1].

The US Consumer Product Safety Commission set guidelines in the 1970s and, since 1991, dryers must have a ground fault circuit interrupter; Wikipedia reports annual deaths fell from fewer than ten to fewer than two by 2000 [1]. The hairbrush article lists early US brush patents: Hugh Rock's modern hairbrush in 1854, Samuel Firey's brush combining elastic wire teeth with natural bristles in 1870, and Lyda D. Newman's improved hairbrush in 1898 [6].

Heat evaporates water from the hair and temporarily breaks hydrogen bonds in keratin. When the hair is cooled while held in a lifted or curved shape by the brush, the bonds re-form in that shape and hold until moisture returns [1][2]. The brush adds tension and root lift; the style resets with washing [1].

In styling descriptions, the brush is passed through a section of damp hair while the airflow follows it, so that the hair dries curved around the barrel and then cools in that shape. Wikipedia notes that a cool-shot button, which blows unheated air, helps set the style and reduces frizz [1]. Wikipedia's hair-straightening article describes a dryer with a comb attachment or round brush on low-to-medium heat, optionally preceded by large rollers on damp hair to reduce heat exposure, and a leave-in conditioner for moisture [2]. Heat-protectant sprays or lotions are described there as potentially reducing damage from heat tools [2].

The blowout is the salon version of the technique. Wikipedia describes the Dominican blowout, which originated in the Dominican Republic and was popularised in the United States by Dominican stylists, as a non-chemical way to straighten hair that is especially popular among African American clients as an alternative to permanent straightening or a way to straighten hair between relaxer treatments [2].

Drybar, a California chain that offers only blowouts, was co-founded by Alli Webb and her brother Michael Landau; its revenue grew from 1.5 million dollars in 2010 to 39 million in 2013, and Helen of Troy acquired the Drybar trademark in 2019 for 255 million dollars, according to Wikipedia [3]. Its own product line launched in Sephora stores and on QVC in 2013 [3].
No studies found on blow-drying with a round brush as an appearance technique in people.

A 2025 laboratory study published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology (Zi and colleagues) washed virgin black Asian hair tresses and ran 30 wet-and-dry cycles with a hair dryer, which the authors equate to a month of daily use. Compared with virgin hair, the dryer-treated tresses showed a lower surface contact angle (about 130 degrees versus about 92 degrees), higher released protein (1.53 versus 1.27 mg/g) and lower tryptophan content, with lifted cuticles on electron microscopy. The authors then created a harsher damage model by oven-heating tresses at 60 degrees Celsius for 24 hours, intended for testing heat-repair products. Only one hair type was tested, in the laboratory, and several authors are affiliated with a company that makes hair products [4].

The main hair-related concern reported in laboratory work is cuticle damage, which increases with heat [4]. Wikipedia's hair-straightening article says excessive or prolonged heat can permanently alter hair structure, that such damage cannot be reversed and can only be disguised or removed by cutting, and that frequent straightening can cause split ends [2]. The hair-care article names heat styling tools among causes of hair damage [5].

Hair dryer burns have been described in case reports; a 1990 Pediatrics report described three children with burn injuries from home hair dryers, one accidental and two inflicted by a caretaker, and prompted testing of home dryers' heat output [7]. Electrical safety features such as ground fault circuit interrupters became mandatory in the US in 1991 [1]. A long-hair forum thread discusses a study comparing dryer use with air-drying [8].

Blow-drying for volume is frequently discussed in men's hair and thinning-hair routines as a styling technique rather than a treatment, and hair-care forums debate heat damage and whether air-drying is gentler [8].

Informal posts show the technique as an everyday routine: one T Nation member describes washing hair and blowing it out straight with a dryer and a round brush as a quick grooming step [9]. A separate T Nation thread on locker rooms jokes that hair dryers should be banned there, a sign of how common they are in gym grooming [10].

Features described in reference sources include ceramic heating elements for rapid heat, a cool-shot button, ionic operation (whose benefit is debated), wattage (modern dryers can draw about 2,000 W), and attachments such as diffusers and concentrators [1]. Round brushes differ in barrel diameter and base material, with the barrel size matched to hair length and the amount of curl or lift wanted [6].

Related heat-styling tools include flat irons, hot combs and electrically heated straightening brushes, which Wikipedia says temporarily change hair's shape until water returns it to its natural state [2]. Large rollers on damp hair, diffusers and air-drying are alternatives mentioned for reducing heat exposure [1][2]. Madam C. J. Walker (1867 to 1919) popularised the straightening comb in the early 1900s, according to the same article [2].

lore.intro: Blow-drying is discussed as a basic technique for adding volume and as a source of heat damage, with threads debating dryer use versus air-drying [8].
